doc.title: Phil Flanigan interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 15, 1998

title: Engineer who called the musicians his tools
summary: A Harry Lim session where an engineer refused Flanigan a microphone on his bass.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: Bass players seem to be at the mercy of the sound people, more than anybody.

Man, I’ve got stories you know. I went into this one session with Butch Miles, the drummer, and this was for Harry Lim, the Famous Door Records guy. And they had a young pony-tailed engineer there, and I had just gotten my new Underwood pick-up, which is good for live situations you know. At the time it seemed, I can play louder now, it’s great. I get in there and we hook it up and we’ve got a direct sound on the thing and we do a little test track, and I said that’s terrible. I mean the pick-up, it’s a good signal and everything, but I hate the sound of it, could I please have a microphone. Maybe then you could mix the two at least, or if not just mix the direct out and leave the microphone the acoustic bass in. He goes, “No you can’t have a microphone.” I said, “Well what’s the © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -9-
matter, don’t you have one? I have one you can use mine.” And the guy says, “No, no, no, no. That sound that you just got? That’s what we want, we’re going to stay with it.

Right. And I said, “Look, that’s not my sound could we compromise?” I wanted to at least talk about it. He got very abrupt and said, “Look buddy, I’m the artist here and you guys are my tools.” And at that point I realized what I was dealing with, that some guy in sound engineer school had propagandized this poor fellow into believing that, and — remember — I could just hear the guy in class saying — now remember, those artists are your tools. You’re the real artist when it comes to the making of a recording.
That’s priceless. That is a classic statement. Wow.
